requirement_groups.source_instruction: The Major in Anthropology Professor Ricky Law, Director of Undergraduate Studies , History Department Location: Baker Hall 238B, 412-268-2880, rlaw@andrew.cmu.edu Dr. Alexandra Garnhart-Bushakra, Academic Program Manager , History Department Location: Baker Hall 240G, 412-268-1260, agarnhar@andrew.cmu.edu Ms. Beth Jameson, M.A., Academic Advisor and Humanities Coordinator , History Department Location: Baker Hall 240A, 412-268-5666, bjameson@andrew.cmu.edu https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/history/undergraduate Overview Anthropology is the study of all forms of human diversity across time and space. The B.A. in Anthropology (ANTHRO) is an interdisciplinary major designed for students who want to understand how societies and cultures are changing in an age of uneven globalization. The rigorous yet flexible curriculum combines courses in anthropology, history, and cultural studies that provide foundational knowledge of both global processes and regional contexts. Anthropology students develop critical skills for working across cultures, analyzing complex problems, and crafting equitable solutions. Graduates of the program have pursued careers in a wide range of fields, including law, education, international development, media, tourism, and community organizing, as well as graduate work in the social sciences, business, public health, medicine, and international relations. Many Anthropology students complete a study-abroad experience during their sophomore or junior years, while others explore a variety of U.S.-based internships and summer research opportunities that embrace pluralistic perspectives. Students should consult with the Academic Program Manager, Dr. Alexandra Garnhart-Bushakra, about new courses and study abroad courses that may be approved for the Anthropology major. Our faculty's expertise in anthropology, history, and environmental studies enables students to develop a rich, multidisciplinary understanding of global issues and concerns (such as, climate change and the environment; inequality; migration; social and political movements; imperial legacies and contemporary politics; art, language, culture, and globalization). Anthropology may be elected as a primary or an additional major; the requirements for each are the same. Curriculum There are two required courses for the major: Introduction to Anthropology ( 79-201 ), and Advanced Seminar in Anthropology ( 79-400 ). In addition to these two courses, majors must also complete 18 units under Topics and Methods in Anthropology, 27 units of Transnational, Global, and Regional Courses, and finally 27 units of electives. Students may “double-count” a maximum of four courses for the Anthropology major that are used to fulfill the requirements of other majors and programs. (Note that some of the courses may have prerequisites established by the departments offering them. Students should consult with the academic advisor about how such prerequisites may affect their course of study.) The Major in Anthropology 93 units I. Anthropology Introductory Course 9 units Students must earn a final grade of "C" or better for the course to count toward the major.

The rigorous yet flexible curriculum combines courses in anthropology, history, and cultural studies that provide foundational knowledge of both global processes and regional contexts. Anthropology students develop critical skills for working across cultures, analyzing complex problems, and crafting equitable solutions. Graduates of the program have pursued careers in a wide range of fields, including law, education, international development, media, tourism, and community organizing, as well as graduate work in the social sciences, business, public health, medicine, and international relations. Many Anthropology students complete a study-abroad experience during their sophomore or junior years, while others explore a variety of U.S.-based internships and summer research opportunities that embrace pluralistic perspectives. Our faculty's expertise in anthropology, history, and environmental studies enables students to develop a rich, multidisciplinary understanding of global issues and concerns (such as, climate change and the environment; inequality; migration; social and political movements; imperial legacies and contemporary politics; art, language, culture, and globalization). Anthropology may be elected as a primary or an additional major; the requirements for each are the same.
